step4.objective:
• Every switch port has a defined untagged (port/access) VLAN at all times, defaulting to the default VLAN, so an unconfigured port is a working untagged member with no additional configuration.
  • A port assigned as untagged member of a single VLAN forwards and learns only that VLAN's traffic; frames for other VLANs are absent from that port.
  • Untagged membership is exclusive — a subsequent port VLAN assignment replaces the previous one rather than accumulating, and the replacement is visible in both the per-port and per-VLAN views.
  • Port VLAN membership survives a reboot and a configuration save/restore cycle, and the restored membership is identical to the configured membership.
  • Removal of a port from a VLAN flushes only the dynamically learned forwarding entries for that VLAN on that port; entries for the same VLAN on other ports, and entries for that port in other VLANs, remain intact and continue to forward.
  • Statically configured filtering entries are added, modified and removed only under explicit management control, and no ageing mechanism removes them — including across a port's membership change.
  • Deletion of a VLAN leaves its former member ports in a deterministic, reported state (returned to the default VLAN or unassigned per platform default) with that VLAN's forwarding entries cleared.
  • Re-creation of a deleted VLAN yields a VLAN with no residual membership, counters or forwarding state from the earlier instance.
  • A VLAN is configurable in an administratively shut-down state; while shut down its member ports pass no traffic in that VLAN, and the administrative state is reported distinctly from port link state. Enabling the VLAN restores forwarding with no re-configuration of membership.
  • Per-port, per-VLAN packet counter instances count only frames belonging to that VLAN on that port, including for an untagged member where the frames carry no tag on the wire; unrelated ports and VLANs are unaffected by the instance.
  • Counter instances are clearable on demand, read back as zero after a clear, and resume accurate counting immediately.
  • The outcome of combining a VLAN counter instance with mirroring on the same port is deterministic and reported — either both functions coexist with correct counts, or the conflicting configuration is rejected with a specific reason and no partial state.
  • Dynamic VLAN classification on a port (subnet or protocol-based) takes documented precedence over the static port VLAN, and the static port VLAN is the fallback when no classifier matches; removing the classifier restores the static membership without a link event.
  • Broadcast, multicast and unknown-unicast flooding for a port's VLAN is confined to that VLAN's member ports, and is re-confined correctly after a dynamic reconfiguration of the classification.
  • Membership changes on one port cause no traffic loss, link transition or forwarding change on other ports or in other VLANs carried on the same device.
  • Invalid port VLAN configuration is rejected with a specific, actionable reason and leaves configuration unchanged: out-of-range or reserved VLAN identifiers, malformed identifier lists, and assignment to a VLAN that does not exist (unless documented auto-creation applies, in which case the created VLAN is reported).
  • Removal of a port from a VLAN it is not a member of, and re-issue of an already-effective assignment, are both benign no-ops that report clearly and change no state.
  • Deletion or removal of the default VLAN, or of the VLAN that a port depends on for its untagged membership while that dependency is in force, is either refused with a reason or completed with the resulting port state explicitly reported.
  • The command-line handler for port VLAN assignment accepts the documented syntax forms — single port, port ranges and lists, and abbreviated keywords — applies each element atomically, and rejects malformed input without applying part of the request.
  • Show output reports VLAN identifier and name, each member port with its tagged/untagged status, and the VLAN administrative state, consistently between per-VLAN and per-port views and consistently with the running configuration.
  • VLAN creation, deletion and port membership changes are observable in the event/log record with enough detail to attribute the change, and forwarding-database views reflect the change immediately after it is applied.

provenance.objective_used:
• Every switch port has a defined untagged (port/access) VLAN at all times, defaulting to the default VLAN, so an unconfigured port is a working untagged member with no additional configuration.
  • A port assigned as untagged member of a single VLAN forwards and learns only that VLAN's traffic; frames for other VLANs are absent from that port.
  • Untagged membership is exclusive — a subsequent port VLAN assignment replaces the previous one rather than accumulating, and the replacement is visible in both the per-port and per-VLAN views.
  • Port VLAN membership survives a reboot and a configuration save/restore cycle, and the restored membership is identical to the configured membership.
  • Removal of a port from a VLAN flushes only the dynamically learned forwarding entries for that VLAN on that port; entries for the same VLAN on other ports, and entries for that port in other VLANs, remain intact and continue to forward.
  • Statically configured filtering entries are added, modified and removed only under explicit management control, and no ageing mechanism removes them — including across a port's membership change.
  • Deletion of a VLAN leaves its former member ports in a deterministic, reported state (returned to the default VLAN or unassigned per platform default) with that VLAN's forwarding entries cleared.
  • Re-creation of a deleted VLAN yields a VLAN with no residual membership, counters or forwarding state from the earlier instance.
  • A VLAN is configurable in an administratively shut-down state; while shut down its member ports pass no traffic in that VLAN, and the administrative state is reported distinctly from port link state. Enabling the VLAN restores forwarding with no re-configuration of membership.
  • Per-port, per-VLAN packet counter instances count only frames belonging to that VLAN on that port, including for an untagged member where the frames carry no tag on the wire; unrelated ports and VLANs are unaffected by the instance.
  • Counter instances are clearable on demand, read back as zero after a clear, and resume accurate counting immediately.
  • The outcome of combining a VLAN counter instance with mirroring on the same port is deterministic and reported — either both functions coexist with correct counts, or the conflicting configuration is rejected with a specific reason and no partial state.
  • Dynamic VLAN classification on a port (subnet or protocol-based) takes documented precedence over the static port VLAN, and the static port VLAN is the fallback when no classifier matches; removing the classifier restores the static membership without a link event.
  • Broadcast, multicast and unknown-unicast flooding for a port's VLAN is confined to that VLAN's member ports, and is re-confined correctly after a dynamic reconfiguration of the classification.
  • Membership changes on one port cause no traffic loss, link transition or forwarding change on other ports or in other VLANs carried on the same device.
  • Invalid port VLAN configuration is rejected with a specific, actionable reason and leaves configuration unchanged: out-of-range or reserved VLAN identifiers, malformed identifier lists, and assignment to a VLAN that does not exist (unless documented auto-creation applies, in which case the created VLAN is reported).
  • Removal of a port from a VLAN it is not a member of, and re-issue of an already-effective assignment, are both benign no-ops that report clearly and change no state.
  • Deletion or removal of the default VLAN, or of the VLAN that a port depends on for its untagged membership while that dependency is in force, is either refused with a reason or completed with the resulting port state explicitly reported.
  • The command-line handler for port VLAN assignment accepts the documented syntax forms — single port, port ranges and lists, and abbreviated keywords — applies each element atomically, and rejects malformed input without applying part of the request.
  • Show output reports VLAN identifier and name, each member port with its tagged/untagged status, and the VLAN administrative state, consistently between per-VLAN and per-port views and consistently with the running configuration.

gaps: The selected ART coverage (2034.16.1) exercises only the static-FDB lifecycle — that statically configured filtering entries are added, modified and removed solely under explicit management control and are exempt from ageing — so it substantiates the deterministic, management-driven half of the forwarding-database behaviour underlying a port VLAN. It does not reach the port-to-VLAN membership semantics that are the substance of this case: selective flushing scoped to just the affected VLAN/port pair when a port leaves a VLAN (AWP-6402, AWPTCM-T9352), untagged-member forwarding with per-port per-VLAN traffic accounting (AWP-6651, AWPTCM-T18166), and broadcast-domain containment as the observable outcome of membership (AWP-14859). Also unautomated are the identity and command-surface boundaries — rejection of an invalid VLAN identifier, the reserved default, and the valid range (AWP-27191, AWPTCM-T18055) — along with the interface-level attach/detach shape drawn from AWP-23330 and the create/delete cycle in AWPTCM-T18076 / AWPTCM-T18208. The state-dependent and reconfiguration-under-load conditions are entirely outside automation: member-port behaviour while the VLAN is administratively shut down (AWP-13704, AWPTCM-T8354), role change of a counted member port to a mirroring role (AWP-6663), and dynamic reconfiguration of an already-populated VLAN (AWPTCM-T18288). Observability is the weakest dimension overall, since the ART item asserts nothing about per-VLAN counter instances or the scope of FDB flush events, both of which currently depend on manual inspection.

• Every switch port has a defined untagged (port/access) VLAN at all times, defaulting to the default VLAN, so an unconfigured port is a working untagged member with no additional configuration.
  • A port assigned as untagged member of a single VLAN forwards and learns only that VLAN's traffic; frames for other VLANs are absent from that port.
  • Untagged membership is exclusive — a subsequent port VLAN assignment replaces the previous one rather than accumulating, and the replacement is visible in both the per-port and per-VLAN views.
  • Port VLAN membership survives a reboot and a configuration save/restore cycle, and the restored membership is identical to the configured membership.
  • Removal of a port from a VLAN flushes only the dynamically learned forwarding entries for that VLAN on that port; entries for the same VLAN on other ports, and entries for that port in other VLANs, remain intact and continue to forward.
  • Statically configured filtering entries are added, modified and removed only under explicit management control, and no ageing mechanism removes them — including across a port's membership change.
  • Deletion of a VLAN leaves its former member ports in a deterministic, reported state (returned to the default VLAN or unassigned per platform default) with that VLAN's forwarding entries cleared.
  • Re-creation of a deleted VLAN yields a VLAN with no residual membership, counters or forwarding state from the earlier instance.
  • A VLAN is configurable in an administratively shut-down state; while shut down its member ports pass no traffic in that VLAN, and the administrative state is reported distinctly from port link state. Enabling the VLAN restores forwarding with no re-configuration of membership.
  • Per-port, per-VLAN packet counter instances count only frames belonging to that VLAN on that port, including for an untagged member where the frames carry no tag on the wire; unrelated ports and VLANs are unaffected by the instance.
  • Counter instances are clearable on demand, read back as zero after a clear, and resume accurate counting immediately.
  • The outcome of combining a VLAN counter instance with mirroring on the same port is deterministic and reported — either both functions coexist with correct counts, or the conflicting configuration is rejected with a specific reason and no partial state.
  • Dynamic VLAN classification on a port (subnet or protocol-based) takes documented precedence over the static port VLAN, and the static port VLAN is the fallback when no classifier matches; removing the classifier restores the static membership without a link event.
  • Broadcast, multicast and unknown-unicast flooding for a port's VLAN is confined to that VLAN's member ports, and is re-confined correctly after a dynamic reconfiguration of the classification.
  • Membership changes on one port cause no traffic loss, link transition or forwarding change on other ports or in other VLANs carried on the same device.
  • Invalid port VLAN configuration is rejected with a specific, actionable reason and leaves configuration unchanged: out-of-range or reserved VLAN identifiers, malformed identifier lists, and assignment to a VLAN that does not exist (unless documented auto-creation applies, in which case the created VLAN is reported).
  • Removal of a port from a VLAN it is not a member of, and re-issue of an already-effective assignment, are both benign no-ops that report clearly and change no state.
  • Deletion or removal of the default VLAN, or of the VLAN that a port depends on for its untagged membership while that dependency is in force, is either refused with a reason or completed with the resulting port state explicitly reported.
  • The command-line handler for port VLAN assignment accepts the documented syntax forms — single port, port ranges and lists, and abbreviated keywords — applies each element atomically, and rejects malformed input without applying part of the request.
  • Show output reports VLAN identifier and name, each member port with its tagged/untagged status, and the VLAN administrative state, consistently between per-VLAN and per-port views and consistently with the running configuration.
  • VLAN creation, deletion and port membership changes are observable in the event/log record with enough detail to attribute the change, and forwarding-database views reflect the change immediately after it is applied.
